traditions/apostolic-christian-assembly/: An indigenous Pentecostal church of Chennai that began in 1948 as a home Bible study led by Pastor G. Sundaram and his wife Beatrice in Purasawalkam. After G. Sundaram's death in 1989, his son M. K. Sam Sundaram became chief pastor and led its growth into one of the best-known Tamil Pentecostal churches; on his death in 2015 he was succeeded by Caleb Joshua. Branches such as Avadi (1973) and K. K. Nagar spread across the city.
Tamil indigenous Pentecostal church with family-led leadership
Mother church at Purasawalkam, Chennai, with daughter congregations
Emphasis on prayer, fasting and healing
Salvation by grace through faith; Spirit baptism with tongues.
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
A chief pastor leading a network of branch churches.
Tamil Pentecostal worship with prayer and testimony.
traditions/presbyterian-church-of-india/: The largest Protestant church of North-East India, headquartered in Shillong. It began when Thomas Jones of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist mission reached Sohra (Cherrapunji) on 22 June 1841, and spread through the Khasi-Jaintia and Lushai (Mizo) hills to Cachar, Manipur and Tripura. A Synod was formed in 1926; in 1953 this became the General Assembly, with the regional assemblies renamed synods, among which the Mizoram Synod is the largest.
Heir of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist mission to the Khasi and Mizo peoples
Khasi and Mizo written languages first put into Roman script by missionaries
Shaped by revivals, notably the Khasi revival of 1905 and repeated Mizo revivals
Synods with strong self-support and mission programmes
Scripture, with the church's confession of faith in the Reformed tradition.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper.
Return of Christ and final judgement.
Presbyterian: presbyteries, synods and a General Assembly.
Reformed worship with strong congregational singing in Khasi, Mizo and other languages.
traditions/council-of-baptist-churches-n: Council of Baptist Churches in North East India

A council of Baptist conventions in North-East India, headquartered in Guwahati. American Baptist missionaries reached Assam in 1836; in January 1950 their work became the Council of Baptist Churches in Assam, later renamed for the whole North-East. Its member conventions serve Assamese, Garo, Naga, Mizo, Karbi, Kuki and other communities.
Umbrella body for many tribal Baptist conventions
Heir of the American Baptist mission begun in 1836
Serves the Garo Baptist Convention and others
Theological training at Eastern Theological College, Jorhat
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Congregational churches in associations and conventions.
Evangelical worship in many local languages.
traditions/nagaland-baptist-church-counc: The council of Baptist churches in Nagaland, headquartered in Kohima. American Baptist work among the Ao Nagas began in the 1870s through the Assamese evangelist Godhula and missionary E. W. Clark; a council of churches was formed in 1937 as the Naga Hills Baptist Church Council. Today it links tribal associations (Ao, Angami, Lotha, Sumi and others) in one of India's few Baptist-majority states.
Represents a Baptist-majority population in Nagaland
Advocacy for alcohol prohibition and for peace in the Naga conflict
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Evangelical worship with strong choral singing.
traditions/evangelical-church-of-india/s: An episcopal evangelical church headquartered in Chennai, which arose from the work of the Oriental Missionary Society (now One Mission Society) and opened its first church in 1954. Under M. Ezra Sargunam (d. 2024), its first bishop, it grew through urban church planting among Tamils and others, reaching his target of 1,000 churches by 1997. It runs the Madras Theological Seminary and College.
traditions/evangelical-church-of-india/d: Indigenous episcopal church from the OMS holiness tradition
Rapid church planting under Ezra Sargunam
traditions/evangelical-church-of-india/p: Salvation by grace through faith and holiness of life.
Evangelical liturgy in Tamil and other languages.
traditions/new-life-fellowship-india/sum: A charismatic church network begun in Pune in 1964 by New Zealand missionaries Graham and Pamela Truscott of the New Life Churches. Established in Mumbai in 1966, it grew under S. Joseph through many small house-based congregations.
traditions/new-life-fellowship-india/pro: Salvation by grace through faith; Spirit baptism.
Believer's baptism and the Lord's Supper.
Network of local churches with central leadership.
traditions/myanmar-baptist-convention/su: The largest Protestant body in Myanmar, formed in 1865 as the Burma Baptist Missionary Convention. It descends from the mission of Adoniram and Ann Hasseltine Judson, who arrived in Rangoon in 1813. Most members belong to ethnic minorities such as Karen, Kachin and Chin.
traditions/myanmar-baptist-convention/pr: Believer's baptism and the Lord's Supper.
traditions/church-of-christ-in-thailand/: Thailand's largest Protestant body, formed in 1934 mainly from the American Presbyterian mission (Bangkok from 1840; Chiang Mai from 1867 under Daniel McGilvary).
Hospitals and schools such as Payap University
traditions/gereja-protestan-indonesia/na: Protestant Church in Indonesia (Gereja Protestan di Indonesia)
traditions/gereja-protestan-indonesia/su: The successor of the Dutch colonial state church (the Indische Kerk), whose roots go back to the first Protestant services in Ambon in 1605. It is now a federation of twelve autonomous churches, including GMIM, GPM, GMIT and GPIB.
traditions/gereja-protestan-indonesia/di: Successor of the colonial state church
Strong in Maluku, Minahasa and Timor
traditions/gereja-protestan-indonesia/pr: Infant baptism and the Lord's Supper.
traditions/sri-lanka-methodist-church/su: Wesleyan missionaries sent with Thomas Coke (who died at sea in 1814) landed at Galle in 1814; the church became an autonomous conference in 1964.
traditions/sri-lanka-methodist-church/di: One of the oldest Methodist churches in Asia
traditions/nondenominational-evangelical: Independent congregations that carry no denominational label, typically evangelical in belief and often contemporary or charismatic in worship. Independent 'Bible churches' existed long before, but the category grew sharply from the 1970s with the Jesus Movement, the church-growth and 'seeker-sensitive' models and the megachurch, until in the United States it became one of the largest Protestant groupings. Similar independent churches are now common across Africa, Latin America and Asia.
No denominational affiliation; each congregation is self-governing, sometimes linked loosely through networks or associations
Short evangelical statements of faith rather than historic confessions
Contemporary worship with bands and projected songs
Many of the largest US megachurches, such as Lakewood Church (Houston) and North Point Community Church (Atlanta), belong to this category
Multi-site campuses and online services led by a founding or senior pastor
The Bible as the inspired and authoritative Word of God, usually set out in a brief local statement of faith; historic creeds are respected but seldom formally adopted.
Salvation by grace through personal faith in Jesus Christ, with emphasis on a conscious decision to follow him ('being born again').
Usually called ordinances: believer's baptism (generally by immersion) and the Lord's Supper as a memorial, often held monthly or less often.
Christ's personal return; many congregations hold a premillennial and pre-tribulation view, though positions vary.
Congregational independence, in practice often led by a senior pastor with a board of elders or trustees.
Informal services centred on contemporary music and a practical sermon; many are openly charismatic, others are not.
traditions/reformed-baptists/summary: A movement of Calvinistic Baptist churches that hold to the Second London Baptist Confession of Faith (1677, adopted by an assembly in 1689). It continues the seventeenth-century Particular Baptist tradition, but as a distinct movement it grew from the Reformed revival of the 1950s and 1960s, helped by the Banner of Truth Trust and by Spurgeon's legacy, in Britain, the United States, South Africa and elsewhere.
traditions/reformed-baptists/distinctive: Subscription to the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689
A Baptist covenant theology ('1689 federalism') distinct from Presbyterian covenant theology
Plural eldership with male elders and deacons
Observance of the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath
Associations such as ARBCA (1997) in North America
traditions/reformed-baptists/profile/aut: Scripture alone as the sufficient and infallible rule, summarised in the 1689 Confession, which opens with its chapter on Scripture.
traditions/reformed-baptists/profile/sal: The doctrines of grace: unconditional election, particular redemption, effectual calling and perseverance, with justification by faith alone.
traditions/reformed-baptists/profile/sac: Two ordinances: baptism of professing believers by immersion and the Lord's Supper, in which believers receive Christ spiritually by faith.
traditions/reformed-baptists/profile/esc: Mostly amillennial or postmillennial, with Christ's return, resurrection and final judgement.
traditions/reformed-baptists/profile/gov: Self-governing congregations led by elders and deacons, cooperating in associations.
traditions/reformed-baptists/profile/wor: Simple services of Scripture reading, prayer, psalms and hymns, and expository preaching.
traditions/reformed-baptists/profile/can: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha is excluded as not inspired.
traditions/primitive-baptists/summary: American 'Old School' Baptists who separated from the missionary Baptists in the 1820s and 1830s. The Kehukee Association in North Carolina condemned missionary societies in 1827, and the Black Rock Address (Maryland, 1832) rejected mission boards, Sunday schools, theological seminaries and other 'modern' institutions as having no warrant in Scripture. They hold a strong doctrine of predestination and keep simple, older forms of worship.
traditions/primitive-baptists/distinctiv: Rejection of missionary societies, Sunday schools and seminaries as unscriptural
A cappella singing, in some areas from shape-note books
Foot washing with the Lord's Supper
Elders who are often unsalaried and self-supporting
Independent churches linked by associations and correspondence
traditions/primitive-baptists/profile/au: Scripture alone; many associations adhere to the London Baptist Confession or their own articles of faith.
traditions/primitive-baptists/profile/sa: God's elect are saved by his sovereign grace; outward means such as missions do not cause regeneration, which is God's direct work.
Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper with unleavened bread and wine, and foot washing.
traditions/primitive-baptists/profile/es: Generally amillennial, with the resurrection and final judgement at Christ's return.
traditions/primitive-baptists/profile/go: Independent congregations led by elders, gathered in local associations.
traditions/primitive-baptists/profile/wo: Plain, unaccompanied singing, extempore preaching and monthly meetings in many rural churches.
traditions/primitive-baptists/profile/ca: The 66-book Protestant canon, traditionally the King James Version.
